## Simple explanation

Regularization discourages a model from fitting training examples too
closely. It can favor simpler solutions that are more likely to work on new
data.

## Technical explanation

Regularization modifies learning through penalties, constraints, or
stochastic procedures. L1 and L2 penalties add terms based on parameter
magnitudes to the objective; dropout and data augmentation are other
regularizing techniques. Their effect depends on model, data, and training
setup.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Reducing overfitting can improve performance on unseen data, especially
when training data is limited or noisy. Regularization choices affect
accuracy, sparsity, calibration, and optimization, so they should be tuned
using validation data.

## How it works

For a parameter vector $\theta$, an L2-regularized objective may be
$L(\theta)+\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2$. The penalty discourages large weights;
$\lambda$ controls its strength. Other methods constrain the hypothesis
space or inject noise during training.

## Practical example

A text classifier that memorizes rare tokens may benefit from an L2 penalty
or dropout. Compare candidate settings on a validation split, then report
the final result on a separate test set.

## Common misconceptions

- Regularization does not guarantee better generalization; too much can
  cause underfitting.
- Weight decay and L2 penalties are closely related but can differ depending
  on the optimizer and parameterization.
